power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps ≤ .036", Text = "Pearson correlations ranged from .349 to .547, and all six individual-model associations remained significant after correction, adjusted ps ≤ .036."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("ps = .058", "p = .792", "ps = .058"), Sentence = c("Associations for Qwen, Terra, and Grok did not survive correction, adjusted ps = .058-.224.", "The ensemble correlation was .343, adjusted p = p = .792.", "Associations for Claude, Qwen, Grok, and Terra did not survive correction, adjusted ps = .058-.311." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential approach to inferring standardized questionnaire responses from qualitative interviews, but their utility for assessing parenting remains unclear.
We evaluated six generative LLMs using zero-shot prompting to infer responses to the Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale (MAPS) from interviews with 43 parents.
Models inferred responses to 35 MAPS items from two introductory questions about family, parenting roles, and the meaning of caregiving.
Performance was evaluated through exact item-response agreement, correlations between inferred and self-reported parenting scores, systematic score differences, and internal consistency.
Across models, Fisher-averaged correlations between inferred and self-reported MAPS subscale scores ranged from .320 to .434, with no consistently superior model.
Correlations were strongest and most consistent for Warmth, whereas Physical Control showed little correspondence and substantial floor restriction.
Across parent-item pairs, 35.5%-44.7% of inferred responses exactly matched parents' selected response categories.
All models assigned systematically lower response categories than parents and rarely selected the highest category; score underestimation was particularly evident for Positive Parenting.
Model-derived subscales generally showed internal consistency, although higher internal consistency did not consistently correspond to stronger correlations with parentreported scores.
Exploratory analyses indicated modest similarity in the associations of inferred and self-reported parenting scores with other psychological constructs.
Preliminary comparisons also suggested that shorter interview segments substantially reduced computational requirements without clear evidence of poorer performance.

These findings support further evaluation of LLM-based parenting assessment while highlighting limitations in reproducing individual responses, matching score levels, and capturing some parenting dimensions.
Parenting is a central context for children's emotional, behavioral, and social development.

Parents' warmth, support, responses to misbehavior, and consistency in setting limits shape children's everyday experiences and are associated with behavioral adjustment across development (Pinquart, 2017).
text.formatted: Parents' warmth, support, responses to misbehavior, and consistency in setting limits shape children's everyday experiences and are associated with behavioral adjustment across development <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Pinquart, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Parenting behaviors also occur within family circumstances that differ in children's developmental needs, caregivers' resources, cultural expectations, and exposure to stress (Belsky, 1984; Rodriguez et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Parenting behaviors also occur within family circumstances that differ in children's developmental needs, caregivers' resources, cultural expectations, and exposure to stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Belsky, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Rodriguez et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These differences present a challenge for assessment: measures must capture meaningful dimensions of parenting while accounting for variation in how behaviors are understood and enacted across families.

Standardized questionnaires are widely used to assess parenting because they offer an efficient approach to assessing multiple domains of parenting using a common set of items and scoring procedures (Parent & Forehand, 2017; Rodriguez et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Standardized questionnaires are widely used to assess parenting because they offer an efficient approach to assessing multiple domains of parenting using a common set of items and scoring procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Parent & Forehand, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Rodriguez et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale (MAPS) organizes parents' reports into interpretable dimensions that can be examined in relation to child and family outcomes (Parent & Forehand, 2017).
text.formatted: For example, the Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale (MAPS) organizes parents' reports into interpretable dimensions that can be examined in relation to child and family outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Parent & Forehand, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Meaningful comparisons across families depend on whether parents interpret items similarly and whether the scores function comparably across groups.

Research on the MAPS has identified measurement nonequivalence across ethnoracial groups and variation in parents' interpretations of MAPS items (Rodriguez, Cadet, et al., 2023; Rodriguez et al., 2025; Rodriguez, La Barrie, et al., 2023; Rodriguez & Shaffer, 2021).
text.formatted: Research on the MAPS has identified measurement nonequivalence across ethnoracial groups and variation in parents' interpretations of MAPS items <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rodriguez, Cadet, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Rodriguez et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Rodriguez, La Barrie, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Rodriguez & Shaffer, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These findings underscore the need to examine how parents interpret standardized items and how the circumstances surrounding parenting behaviors inform their responses.

Qualitative interviews allow parents to describe parenting in their own terms, including the challenges they encounter, how they interpret their children's behavior, and the considerations that guide their responses (Rodriguez, Cadet, et al., 2023; Rodriguez et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Qualitative interviews allow parents to describe parenting in their own terms, including the challenges they encounter, how they interpret their children's behavior, and the considerations that guide their responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rodriguez, Cadet, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Rodriguez et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These accounts can illuminate connections among parenting behaviors, emotional experiences, and social circumstances, while allowing parents to emphasize experiences that researchers may not have anticipated (Daly, 2003; Gilgun, 2012).
text.formatted: These accounts can illuminate connections among parenting behaviors, emotional experiences, and social circumstances, while allowing parents to emphasize experiences that researchers may not have anticipated <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Daly, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gilgun, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Alongside their value for understanding these experiences, interviews raise a complementary measurement question: to what extent do parents' narratives convey information about the parenting dimensions assessed by standardized questionnaires?

Computational text analysis offers tools for examining this question (Janasik et al., 2009) with prior applications identifying common parenting concerns in online discussions (Westrupp et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Computational text analysis offers tools for examining this question <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Janasik et al., 2009)</ref> with prior applications identifying common parenting concerns in online discussions <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Westrupp et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Extending this approach to estimate questionnaire responses from individual interviews requires evaluating how closely those estimates correspond to parents' questionnaire reports.
This comparison can identify which parenting dimensions are reflected in parents' narrative accounts.
Generative large language models (LLMs) offer a potential approach to translating narrative information into standardized item responses.
Recent work has used zero-shot prompting to infer personality questionnaire responses from open-ended narratives without taskspecific model training (Peters & Matz, 2024; Wright et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent work has used zero-shot prompting to infer personality questionnaire responses from open-ended narratives without taskspecific model training <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Peters & Matz, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Wright et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A model can be given an interview transcript, the wording of a questionnaire item, and a defined set of response options, then asked to infer the response best supported by the narrative.
This approach can be evaluated using existing interview datasets without first assembling a labeled sample for task-specific training.
Its usefulness, however, depends on whether the resulting responses agree with relevant comparison measures and whether errors reveal systematic distortions (Fan et al., 2023; Speer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Its usefulness, however, depends on whether the resulting responses agree with relevant comparison measures and whether errors reveal systematic distortions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Fan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Speer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work on personality assessment provides examples of this approach. Wright et al. (2026) used seven generative LLMs to assess Big Five personality traits from spontaneous streams of thought and daily video diaries across two samples (Wright et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent work on personality assessment provides examples of this approach. <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Wright et al. (2026)</ref> used seven generative LLMs to assess Big Five personality traits from spontaneous streams of thought and daily video diaries across two samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Wright et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Modelderived scores converged with self-reported personality and showed associations with daily behaviors and mental health outcomes, although performance differed across models.
These findings suggest that narrative data can contain information relevant to standardized psychological assessment.
Extending this framework to parenting requires a separate empirical test.
Parenting practices are relational and context dependent (Sameroff, 2010).
text.formatted: Parenting practices are relational and context dependent <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Sameroff, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, interviews and questionnaires both rely on parental disclosure.
Comparing interviews and questionnaires evaluates correspondence between two formats of parental report.

Evaluating several model families is particularly useful when adapting narrative scoring to a new assessment domain. Wright et al. (2026) found that personality-assessment performance varied across models and that averaging model scores produced the strongest agreement with self-report in their study (Wright et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Evaluating several model families is particularly useful when adapting narrative scoring to a new assessment domain. <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Wright et al. (2026)</ref> found that personality-assessment performance varied across models and that averaging model scores produced the strongest agreement with self-report in their study <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Wright et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A comparison using common transcripts and item targets can establish how dependent parenting-score convergence is on the selected model.
Agreement among models may identify consistently inferred responses, while disagreement may reveal ambiguity or sensitivity to model-specific assumptions.
However, consensus alone does not establish accuracy, because models may share errors (Kim et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, consensus alone does not establish accuracy, because models may share errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kim et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Performance must therefore be evaluated against parents' questionnaire responses for each model, and any combined scoring approach requires its own evaluation.
An additional question concerns how much narrative information is needed to infer parenting scores.
A longer-term goal is to reduce assessment burden by using brief spoken accounts to obtain information about multiple parenting dimensions.
In daily assessment, parents could describe their experiences in an audio recording that is transcribed and scored, potentially reducing the number of separate questionnaire responses required.
Developing this approach requires determining how much narrative material is sufficient and whether particular dimensions benefit from targeted prompts.
Additional interview content may provide useful behavioral examples and context, but it also increases collection burden and the amount of text processed by a model.
Additional content may be redundant or introduce information less relevant to the assessment target (Liu et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Additional content may be redundant or introduce information less relevant to the assessment target <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Liu et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Shi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Comparing brief segments with full interviews provides an initial test of how narrative length and content relate to scoring performance and computational requirements.
The role of interviewer speech also warrants examination.
Interviewer questions can clarify what a parent is responding to and help resolve brief or ambiguous answers.
Conversely, those questions may introduce language about parenting practices that the parent does not endorse (Holstein & Gubrium, 1995).
text.formatted: Conversely, those questions may introduce language about parenting practices that the parent does not endorse <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Holstein & Gubrium, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Retaining interviewer turns could thus improve interpretation or influence predictions through content supplied by the interviewer rather than the parent.

Comparing full dialogue with versions that omit interviewer turns offers a way to examine whether this contextual information improves agreement and whether its contribution justifies the additional text.
The present study uses qualitative interviews to evaluate whether multiple LLMs can infer parents' responses to MAPS items from their narrative accounts.
Our first objective is to characterize agreement with parents' questionnaire responses and examine whether performance differs across models and parenting dimensions.
We evaluate exact item matches, prediction error, correlations between inferred and self-reported scores, systematic score differences, and internal consistency.

Our second objective is to examine how transcript length and inclusion of interviewer speech relate to prediction performance alongside text and computational requirements, informing future development of brief narrative assessments.

Eligible participants were at least 18 years old, resided in the United States, had a child between 0 and 18 years of age, and completed an interview in English.

Parents' mean age was 37.7 years (SD = 6.9; range = 27-54), and children's ages ranged from 0 to 17 years.

We conducted 60-90-minute parenting interviews remotely through the laboratory's HIPAA-compliant Zoom account.
Study staff reviewed automated transcripts against the recordings to correct transcription errors and speaker labels while preserving participants' wording.
Study staff also prepared separate versions excluding interviewer speech.

Study staff labeled transcripts with assigned study identifiers and manually removed information that could identify participants, their children, or others mentioned in the interviews while preserving the substantive parenting content wherever possible.
Staff checked the transcripts for remaining identifying information before submitting them to the LLMs for scoring.
Prior to the main analysis, we conducted preliminary comparisons using interviews from 15 parents to select an efficient transcript format for the main analysis.

Using Qwen and Gemini, we compared four formats: full interviews with both speakers (interviewers and parents), full interviews with parent speech only, introductory (e.g., rapport-building warm-up) segments with both speakers, and introductory segments with parent speech only.
Introductory segments comprised responses to two questions: "Can you tell me a little about your family and your role as a parent?"
and "What does being a parent/caregiver mean to you?"
These comparisons examined prediction performance, computational requirements, and the amount of transcript material submitted for scoring.
We selected parent-only introductory segments and supplied the same text to all six models in the main analysis.
Across these 15 interviews, full dialogue contained 176,358 words (M = 11,757 per parent), and introductory dialogue contained 32,774 words (M = 2,185).
Removing interviewer speech reduced these totals to 130,375 and 26,084 words, respectively.
Based on preliminary comparisons in a subset of 15 parents, we selected parent-only introductory segments for the main analysis of all 43 parents.
This format reduced scoring costs and computational demands while limiting the amount of interview text shared with the models.
Six LLMs were accessed through OpenRouter, representing OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, Meta, and Alibaba.
The model set included both proprietary and open-weight models.

The model set included four proprietary models: GPT-5.6 Terra (openai/gpt-5.6-terra), Claude Sonnet 5 (anthropic/claude-sonnet-5), Gemini 3.8 Flash (google/gemini-3.8-flash), and Grok 4.7 (x-ai/grok-4.7), and two open-weight models: Llama 4 Maverick (meta-llama/llama-4-maverick) and Qwen3 235B A22B 2507 (qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507).

text.text: Requests were submitted through OpenRouter with zerodata-retention routing required (zdr=True) and provider data collection disabled (data_collection="deny"); no specific upstream inference provider was manually pinned.
For each parent, each model inferred responses to the 35 MAPS items using the parentonly introductory transcript.
Parents' self-reported MAPS responses were withheld from all scoring inputs.
Each participant-item pair was scored in a separate request with a fresh context.
Models received the interview text, target child age, target MAPS item, and the five permitted response options.

They were instructed to respond as though they were the interviewed parent, base their response on parenting practices and behaviors inferable from the interview, answer with respect to the target child and the previous two months, and focus on the target child when multiple children were discussed.
Responses were constrained to exactly one of Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, or Always, with no explanation, punctuation, or additional text.
Responses were subsequently mapped to numerical scores from 1 to 5, respectively.
The same prompt wording was used across all six models; only model-specific inference settings differed where supported.
No separate system prompt was used.
The complete scoring prompt is provided in the Supplementary Materials.
Performance was evaluated at the item, subscale, and broader parenting dimension levels (i.e., negative parenting and positive parenting).
At the item level, mean absolute error (MAE) was calculated as the mean absolute difference between inferred and self-reported responses.

Exact agreement was the percentage of inferred responses matching the corresponding selfreported response, and agreement within one category was the percentage differing by no more than one response category.
Signed error was calculated as the inferred response minus the selfreported response; negative values indicated numerically lower inferred responses.
Because MAPS items assess both positive and negative parenting behaviors, the direction of numerical error was interpreted separately from the favorability of the behavior assessed.
Item-level metrics were calculated using all usable predictions for each model.
There were 1,505 possible participant-item pairs per model in the main sample and 525 pairs per condition in the 15-parent Qwen transcript-selection analysis.
Missing or unusable responses were excluded from the corresponding metric denominators.

When one or more constituent item responses were missing, subscale scores were calculated as the mean of the remaining usable items, consistent with the MAPS scoring procedure; a subscale score was treated as missing only if none of its constituent items had a usable response.
MAPS subscale scores were calculated as the mean of their constituent items on the 1-5 Likert scale.

Positive Parenting was calculated as the mean of Proactive Parenting, Positive Reinforcement, Warmth, and Supportiveness; Negative Parenting was calculated as the mean of Hostility, Lax Control, and Physical Control.
Pearson correlations quantified convergence between inferred and self-reported scores across parents.
Spearman correlations were also calculated to assess rank-order convergence.
Absolute agreement was evaluated using Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, MAE, and signed error at the subscale level.
Broadband analyses included Pearson and Spearman correlations and signed error.

Overall construct convergence was summarized by Fisher z transforming the Pearson correlations for the six subscales with estimable correlations across all models, averaging the transformed coefficients, and transforming the mean back to the correlation scale.
Physical Control was excluded from this summary because several models produced invariant scores.
Correlations were not estimated for model-subscale combinations with no between-participant variation.
For the main construct-level analyses, we calculated each parent's MAPS subscale scores separately for each of the six models, applying the missing-item scoring rule within each model.
We then averaged the six model-specific scores for each subscale to obtain the parent's ensemble subscale score.
We evaluated the ensemble scores using the same construct-level analyses as the individual-model scores.

Two-sided Pearson correlation tests were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, separately across the 46 estimable model-by-subscale associations and the 14 model-by-broadband associations, including the ensemble.
Lin's concordance correlation coefficient was used to assess how closely model-inferred and selfreported scores matched in both their between-parent variation and absolute values.
Confidence intervals were estimated using 10,000 participant-level bootstrap resamples.
Each resample retained all item responses from each selected parent, preserving the dependence among observations within parents.
Conventional Pearson tests and bootstrap confidence intervals were reported alongside Spearman correlations to characterize associations that differed across these approaches.
Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha for each MAPS subscale based on parent-reported responses and each model's item predictions.

For the ensemble, we averaged the available predictions across models for each participant-item pair, retained the resulting values without rounding, and calculated alpha from these item-level averages.
Alpha was not reported when insufficient response variance prevented estimation.
Exploratory nomological validity analyses examined whether LLM-inferred MAPS scores preserved associations with theoretically relevant external psychological constructs.
For the ensemble nomological analysis, we first averaged the available model predictions for each participant-item pair and then calculated MAPS subscale scores from those item-level averages.

Correspondence between the resulting nomological profiles was evaluated using profile correlations and mean absolute differences between corresponding associations, with 95% confidence intervals estimated from 10,000 participant-level bootstrap resamples.
We also conducted an exploratory analysis to examine whether disagreement across LLMs was associated with prediction error.
Cross-model disagreement was quantified as the standard deviation of the available model predictions for each participant-item combination and examined in relation to ensemble absolute error.
The association between cross-model disagreement and ensemble absolute error was evaluated using a linear mixed-effects model with crossed random intercepts for participant and MAPS item.
For each participant-item pair, ensemble absolute error was the absolute difference between the mean of the available model predictions and the corresponding parent-reported MAPS response.

MAE was calculated for each parent in each condition.

Paired differences were defined as MAE for the reduced representation minus MAE for the more complete representation; positive values therefore indicated lower error when additional content was retained.

Mean paired differences and 95% confidence intervals were estimated using the participant-level bootstrap procedure described above, retaining each parent's paired condition scores within all 10,000 resamples.
Confidence intervals were calculated using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution.
Confidence intervals containing zero were not interpreted as demonstrating equivalence or noninferiority.
At the item level, inferred responses were classified as unchanged or changed across conditions.
Changed responses were further classified according to whether their absolute error decreased, increased, or remained equal relative to the corresponding self-reported response.
These descriptive comparisons were considered alongside paired MAE differences and computational requirements when selecting the introductory, parent-only representation for the main analysis.

Textual inputs and computational requirements were summarized using prompt-token counts and monetary costs for the available scoring runs.
For each model and transcript condition, summaries were based on the complete set of 525 participant-item scoring records from the 15-parent preliminary sample.
Prompt-token counts and monetary costs were taken from the usage metadata returned by OpenRouter for each successful request and summed across requests within each condition.

Percentage reductions in prompt tokens and cost were calculated separately relative to the full-dialogue condition within each model because tokenization, model pricing, and completion usage differed across models.
Reported costs therefore represent the recorded billed cost associated with each returned request.
Costs from any preceding failed or retried requests were not separately accumulated in these summaries.

text.text: This study evaluated whether six large language models could infer parents' MAPS questionnaire responses from the parent-only introductory segments of qualitative interviews.
All models showed positive overall convergence with parent self-report, although performance varied across parenting dimensions and evaluation metrics.
Warmth showed the most consistent convergence, whereas associations for Hostility, Supportiveness, and Lax Control depended more on the model.
Proactive Parenting and Positive Reinforcement showed stronger Pearson than Spearman correlations, with bootstrap intervals indicating considerable uncertainty.
Physical Control showed little convergence and substantial restriction in both self-reported and inferred scores.
Across models, positive construct-level associations coexisted with limited exact item agreement and systematically lower inferred response categories.

These findings extend research examining LLM-based inference of psychological characteristics from narrative data to the assessment of parenting (Fan et al., 2023; Peters & Matz, 2024; Wright et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These findings extend research examining LLM-based inference of psychological characteristics from narrative data to the assessment of parenting <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Fan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Peters & Matz, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Wright et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The clearest evidence of convergence emerged for Warmth, for which every model showed positive associations supported by conventional tests, bootstrap confidence intervals, and rank correlations.

One possible explanation is that parents' descriptions of their families and the meaning of caregiving convey relational information relevant to warmth even without direct questions about specific behaviors.

This interpretation is consistent with approaches that assess representations of caregiving and parent-child relationships through parental narratives (Rodriguez, Cadet, et al., 2023; Rodriguez et al., 2025; Rodriguez, La Barrie, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with approaches that assess representations of caregiving and parent-child relationships through parental narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rodriguez, Cadet, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Rodriguez et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Rodriguez, La Barrie, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Future work could examine whether inferred warmth reflects explicit descriptions of affectionate behavior, broader expressions of connection, or other features of parents' narratives.
Findings for the remaining dimensions were less consistent.
Hostility and Supportiveness showed convergence for several models, whereas Lax Control was more dependent on the model selected.
Supportiveness also had comparatively low internal consistency in parent self-report, introducing uncertainty into the comparison measure.
Measurement error in a comparison measure can constrain observed convergence (Schmidt & Hunter, 1996).
text.formatted: Measurement error in a comparison measure can constrain observed convergence <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Schmidt & Hunter, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Differences in convergence therefore may reflect a combination of narrative coverage, model inference, and the measurement properties of the self-reported subscales.
The current design cannot isolate the contribution of each.
These findings also build on prior work demonstrating the importance of examining how parents understand assessment items.
Cognitive interviews used to revise the MAPS identified difficulties involving item wording, interpretations of affection, and descriptions of disciplinary practices (Rodriguez et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Cognitive interviews used to revise the MAPS identified difficulties involving item wording, interpretations of affection, and descriptions of disciplinary practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Rodriguez et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although the present study examined model inference rather than questionnaire revision, both approaches highlight the importance of the information available when translating parenting experiences into standardized responses.
Future research could examine whether items that parents interpret inconsistently are also more difficult for models to infer from narrative accounts.
Proactive Parenting and Positive Reinforcement warrant particular attention because their Pearson correlations suggested stronger convergence than their rank correlations and bootstrap intervals.
These discrepancies indicate that conclusions depended on how convergence was evaluated.
Positive linear associations did not consistently translate into stable ordering of parents across the score distribution.

Pearson correlations can be sensitive to influential observations and distributional characteristics, making complementary analyses useful when evaluating convergence (Bishara & Hittner, 2012; Pernet et al., 2013; Wilcox, 2012).
text.formatted: Pearson correlations can be sensitive to influential observations and distributional characteristics, making complementary analyses useful when evaluating convergence <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bishara & Hittner, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Pernet et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Wilcox, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: With only 43 participants, individual observations may have considerable influence on correlation estimates.
Larger samples would allow more precise evaluation of these dimensions, including the influence of individual observations and performance across different score ranges.
Physical Control illustrates a different measurement problem.
Nearly three quarters of parents reported scores at the scale minimum, and three models assigned the same subscale score to every parent.
Under these conditions, small absolute errors can arise from predictions concentrated near the floor without successful differentiation among parents.
Restricted score variation can also attenuate correlations and complicate the interpretation of predictive performance (Branco et al., 2016; Sackett & Yang, 2000; Terwee et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Restricted score variation can also attenuate correlations and complicate the interpretation of predictive performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Branco et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Sackett & Yang, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Terwee et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Evaluating this sample and transcript segment provided a limited test.
Evaluating this dimension will require samples with greater behavioral variation and interview content that provides opportunities to discuss disciplinary practices.
Models sometimes captured between-parent differences in broader parenting scores while exactly matching fewer than half of parents' individual item responses.
Model rankings also changed across these measures.
Llama, for example, showed one of the largest average subscale correlations but the lowest percentage of exact item matches.
A positive correlation indicates that parents with higher self-reported scores generally also received higher model-inferred scores.
Those inferred scores can still be systematically higher or lower than parents' reports.

Correlations therefore provide information about relative differences among parents, while exact item matches and score differences indicate how closely models reproduce parents' responses (Bland & Altman, 1986; Lin, 1989).
text.formatted: Correlations therefore provide information about relative differences among parents, while exact item matches and score differences indicate how closely models reproduce parents' responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bland & Altman, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Lin, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Exploratory analyses examined whether model-inferred parenting scores showed similar associations with other psychological measures as parent-reported parenting scores.
These associations were only partly preserved, with several correlations differing in magnitude or direction.
Thus, models' correlations with parent-reported MAPS scores provided an incomplete picture of how the inferred scores related to other constructs (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955).
text.formatted: Thus, models' correlations with parent-reported MAPS scores provided an incomplete picture of how the inferred scores related to other constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cronbach & Meehl, 1955)</ref>.

text.text: The small sample and shared reliance on parent reports across the questionnaire measures may have contributed to these differences.
Systematic score differences also helped explain the results.
Every model assigned numerically lower item responses on average than parents, and selected the highest response category substantially less often.
Every model underestimated Positive Parenting, whereas differences in Negative Parenting varied across models, with some showing average differences close to zero.
Lower responses indicated less frequent endorsement of the behavior being assessed, so their substantive meaning depended on whether the items described positive or negative parenting practices.
Several explanations may account for these differences.
Parental questionnaire responses can be influenced by recall, response formats, and socially desirable responding in parental selfreport (Morsbach & Prinz, 2006).
text.formatted: Parental questionnaire responses can be influenced by recall, response formats, and socially desirable responding in parental selfreport <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Morsbach & Prinz, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Models may also interpret response categories differently when working from narrative accounts, particularly when high-frequency ratings require explicit evidence about how often a behavior occurs.
The introductory interview segment may provide limited examples of such behaviors.
Future comparisons with repeated reports and behavioral observations could help distinguish these explanations.
The combined Positive Parenting score correlated more consistently with parent reports than the combined Negative Parenting score.

Averaging across positive parenting dimensions may have reduced some variation specific to individual items or subscales, consistent with measurement principles concerning aggregation (Rushton et al., 1983).
text.formatted: Averaging across positive parenting dimensions may have reduced some variation specific to individual items or subscales, consistent with measurement principles concerning aggregation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Rushton et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Results nevertheless varied among the dimensions contributing to each combined score.

Positive Parenting included some positive subscales with less consistent correlations, while Negative Parenting combined dimensions with substantially different score distributions and correlations with parent reports.
Positive overall convergence across six model families suggests that the observed associations were not confined to one model.
Nevertheless, no model had the largest point estimates across all constructs and metrics, and the ensemble did not exceed the strongest individual models in overall convergence.

Model selection should therefore reflect the intended parenting dimension and whether the priority is stronger correlations with parent reports, smaller prediction errors, or closer matching of score levels.
Greater disagreement across models was associated with higher ensemble prediction error, suggesting that cross-model variability may provide a limited indicator of prediction uncertainty (Table S8).
text.formatted: Greater disagreement across models was associated with higher ensemble prediction error, suggesting that cross-model variability may provide a limited indicator of prediction uncertainty (Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>).

text.text: Shared systematic errors remain a consideration when using agreement among models to estimate prediction uncertainty ( (Kim et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Shared systematic errors remain a consideration when using agreement among models to estimate prediction uncertainty ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kim et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Most model-generated subscales showed coherent internal consistency, but this coherence did not consistently correspond to stronger convergence with parent self-report.

For Physical Control, the item-level ensemble showed high internal consistency (α = .865), while the ensemble formed by averaging model-specific subscale scores showed negligible convergence with parent self-report (r = .045).
These estimates address distinct questions about the coherence of the averaged item predictions and the correspondence of the aggregated subscale scores with parent reports.
Evaluating both provides a fuller account of score performance (Clark & Watson, 1995; Messick, 1995; Sijtsma, 2009).
text.formatted: Evaluating both provides a fuller account of score performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Clark & Watson, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Messick, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Sijtsma, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Internally consistent predictions can therefore organize item responses coherently while failing to capture the corresponding differences among parents.
Reliability estimates should be considered alongside external agreement rather than treated as sufficient evidence of successful assessment.
The findings support further investigation of LLM scoring as a complementary way to quantify information from parenting interviews.

Previous research has used computational text analysis to identify common parenting concerns in online discussions (Westrupp et al., 2022), and methodological work has examined how text mining can complement qualitative analysis (Janasik et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Previous research has used computational text analysis to identify common parenting concerns in online discussions <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Westrupp et al., 2022)</ref>, and methodological work has examined how text mining can complement qualitative analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Janasik et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The present study addressed a different task: inferring standardized parenting questionnaire responses from individual parents' narratives.
This application offers a way to examine connections between narrative accounts and established measures, particularly when qualitative data have already been collected.
Linking inferred scores to the original narratives could help researchers examine how parents' descriptions of specific experiences relate to broader parenting dimensions.
Future studies should evaluate whether these scores help explain child and family outcomes and how they can complement qualitative analyses of the same interviews.
These findings motivate testing brief daily audio accounts as a potentially lower-burden approach to repeated parenting assessment.
A central question is how much audio is needed to infer each parenting dimension.
Studies could vary recording duration, the questions parents answer, and the number of days sampled to identify efficient combinations of narrative length and behavioral coverage.
Comparisons with daily questionnaires and behavioral observations could examine both differences among parents and changes within the same parent across days.
Completion time, adherence, and parents' perceived burden would provide direct evidence of the practical benefits of this approach.
Further development should distinguish explicit behavioral evidence from inference based on limited information.
Allowing models to indicate insufficient evidence, identify supporting passages, or express uncertainty may help clarify when a questionnaire response is supported by the transcript.

Evaluation could test whether supporting passages and uncertainty estimates help identify predictions with larger errors (Farquhar et al., 2024; Turpin et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Evaluation could test whether supporting passages and uncertainty estimates help identify predictions with larger errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Farquhar et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Turpin et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Wen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Xiong et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Any systematic score differences procedure should be developed and evaluated in separate samples.
Comparisons with simple prediction baselines and trained human coders would also help establish the added value of LLM scoring relative to less complex approaches.
Several limitations are warrant discussions.
The sample included 43 parents, limiting precision and the ability to evaluate differences across demographic groups, child developmental stages, or family contexts.
The large number of item predictions did not increase the number of independent participants.
Floor and ceiling concentrations further limited the range of parenting behaviors represented.

Prior research has documented limited evaluation of parenting measures across racial and ethnic groups and identified measurement nonequivalence in the MAPS (Rodriguez, Cadet, et al., 2023; Rodriguez, La Barrie, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Prior research has documented limited evaluation of parenting measures across racial and ethnic groups and identified measurement nonequivalence in the MAPS <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rodriguez, Cadet, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Rodriguez, La Barrie, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These findings underscore the need to evaluate both the questionnaire comparison measure and model-inferred scores across populations.
Replication should include larger and more heterogeneous samples, including interviews conducted in languages other than English.
Overall convergence should be supplemented by direct examination of subgroup differences in error, systematic score differences, and construct convergence.
Both the interviews and questionnaires relied on the same parent as the source of information.
Their convergence may partly reflect shared perceptions, disclosure patterns, or presentation of parenting across formats.
A multitrait-multimethod perspective emphasizes the need to distinguish evidence about the intended constructs from effects associated with the assessment methods (Campbell & Fiske, 1959).
text.formatted: A multitrait-multimethod perspective emphasizes the need to distinguish evidence about the intended constructs from effects associated with the assessment methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959)</ref>.

text.text: Without observational assessments, other informants, or external criteria, these results cannot establish correspondence with independently assessed parenting behavior.
Future studies should examine convergence with coparent and youth reports, observational measures, and relevant child and family outcomes.
Repeated assessments could establish the temporal stability of inferred scores and their sensitivity to changes in parenting.
Preliminary comparisons supported selecting parent-only introductory segments for the assessment targets examined here.
Replication in an independent sample would help establish how well this transcript-selection approach generalizes (Cawley & Talbot, 2010; Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017).
text.formatted: Replication in an independent sample would help establish how well this transcript-selection approach generalizes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cawley & Talbot, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies can extend this work by testing stand-alone brief interview or dailu audio recordings.
The current findings therefore do not demonstrate that shorter interviews and examining how interviewer speech contributes to scoring across assessment targets.
Repeated scoring runs and alternative prompts, and independently evaluated transcript-selection procedures would further clarify the reproducibility of the approach.
LLM-inferred scores from parents' introductory interview narratives correlated with several self-reported parenting dimensions, with the most consistently Warmth and combined Positive Parenting.
Performance varied across dimensions, and models tended to assign lower response categories than parents.
These findings provide an initial basis for developing brief narrative approaches to parenting assessment.

Testing how much spoken information is needed for different dimensions, and whether brief daily recordings reduce burden while capturing changes in parenting, offers a practical direction for further development.
